I just finished a playthrough, and boy was it fun. Rewarding too, since the game can be quite challenging. The game has a lighthearted anime aesthetic, but don't let this distract you from the gameplay - a mixture of Metroidvania and bullet hell. For those who don't know:

  • "Metroidvania" refers to an open-ended style of game progression, where the player traverses a large interconnected world rather than a series of isolated levels. The player will usually open up new areas through items discovered during exploration, and sometimes RPG leveling mechanics are present. The most obvious examples are Super Metroid and Castlevania:SOTN.

  • "Bullet hell" refers to a genre where enemies launch huge amounts of projectiles at the player, to the point where the projectiles seem unavoidable. However, because the player's hitbox is tiny and the attack patterns are predictable, the player can avoid taking damage with decent reflexes and solid analytical skills. Touhou is probably the most popular example of this genre.

Rabi-Ribi mixes these together, producing a 2D platformer that anyone can enjoy. For those of you who don't like bullet hell, the easiest difficulty removes a lot of pressure and lets you easily explore the world. But for those who enjoy a challenge, even "Novice" difficulty can give you a run for your money. The best part is that there's a demo!

http://rabiribi.kano-bi.com/demo

I don't usually post here about the games I play, but I feel like this game really deserves the publicity. We don't get too many quality Metroidvanias today.
Check out Rabi-Ribi, a new indie title that mixes Super Metroid, moe anime girls and punishing difficulty.

Alright... Last I heard, BTRFS was the "leading" file system for the next gen... Why is Canonical pushing the underdog here?

This seems to be more of Canonical's MO: we saw it with Wayland/Mir, SysVInit/Systemd/UpStart, UCC/KCC, Unity/Gnome, and now with entire file systems?

Why does Canonical feel the need to mess with everything, and pet AGAINST the grain?

EDIT: Alright, I did some digging, because I wanted some facts behind my comments instead of an off-the-wall, old news comment.

Apparently, even the creators of ZFS (Oracle - Sun Microsystems) has stopped funding ZFS and is now supporting BTRFS both morally as well as financially. This is pretty big to me, as it says what ZFS's creators think about the project. Of course, there's an OpenZFS project in the works, but these are NOT the same.

ZFS is also licensed under the Common Development and Distribution License (otherwise known as the CDDL), whereas the Linux kernel is licensed under the GPLv2 agreement. These two are incompatible, and therefore ZFS can NEVER be packaged with the Linux kernel... Ubuntu is packaging it with their distro, but ZFS isn't supported on a kernel level.

In comparison, BTRFS is licensed under GPL with the Linux kernel... which you can discern the outcome of that compatibility and partnership, as well as its benefits.

ZFS currently has more features, but with the legitimate lack of funding for it (and the proper funding sources behind BTRFS), those "additional" features are becoming more and more negligible as BTRFS catches up (and begins to surpass) with ZFS in terms of both stability as well as features.

I just don't see the benefit of Canonical throwing in with a sub-par file system which is going to remain stagnant, according to its creators and their intentions. Why wouldn't they support the file system which actually has potential?

I'm not asking these questions to be a dick... I legitimately want answers. I've been a Linux user for the better part of a decade, and my first distro was Ubuntu... and I stuck with a *buntu flavor for the majority of my Linux "career," but I have never understood Canonical's business strategies, or why they make the backwards decisions they do.

Most people aren't going to use a RAID array... especially users of Ubuntu.

ZFS, in that instance, provides no enhancement over EXT or BTRFS.

Additionally, BTRFS is funded and ZFS is not (as I stated). This means that ZFS will be obsolete in no time as it is currently stagnant and abandoned by it's creators (Oracle). On the other hand, as you pointed out, BTRFS will continue to be developed and worked on in a progressive way... ultimately incorporating RAID5/6 system support, as well as future hardware systems.

ZFS is a enterprise filesystem. The official ZFS documentation tells you to not use it as average home user. ZFS development now happens in OpenZFS which has a lot of sponsors and no funding problems. Many of the OpenZSF commiters are employed by companies using the filesystem. And for most that means they use it in multimillion dollar server farms. That's what zfs is made for. This companies will be using zfs for years to come, because you just don't change such large setups just because some new fs developers now tell you their fs works as good as the one you use. Just take a look at the sponsors of last year's OpenZSF summit to grasp who is backing that. http://open-zfs.org/wiki/OpenZFS_Developer_Summit

ZFS is a enterprise filesystem for large storage uses mainly. If you don't have RAID, it is 95% the wrong fs for you. If you have a machine without ECC RAM, you should absolutely not use ZFS there.
